primary_claim: A new SAE feature-label generation method (baez) that uses NLA explanations instead of activation examples performs about as well as the standard eleuther_acts_top5 method, but both methods score close to chance on detection, fuzz, and embedding evals, suggesting either the labeling methods or the evals themselves are broken.

effect.metric: detection/fuzz eval score (fraction correct) and embedding cosine gap
effect.value: mean detection/fuzz scores close to chance for baez, baez_last, and eleuther_acts_top5 alike; embedding gaps tiny (~0.01-0.02 cosine), ~40% of labels show a negative gap

contradicts_or_qualifies: Cites Robert_AIZI's comment that labels generated from top-activating examples fail to capture the long tail of lower-activating examples as an explanation for why eleuther_acts_top5 scored near chance in this train/test split
stated_future_work: try new label-generation approaches until one performs well on these evals
analyze a task that actually requires feature labels and build the label generation method accordingly
apply the proposed tier-based score-then-label protocol to an actual attribution graph experiment
limitations_stated: the [0,4] train vs [5,15] test activation-example split was inadequate
baez labels are derived from an NLA activation layer far from input tokens, which may explain its poor performance on evals that measure correlation with input activation examples
the proposed tier-based labeling protocol is untested
quote: the results show that baez ≈ eleuther_acts_top5 across all the evals, despite using different inputs (NLA explanations vs. activation examples). Perhaps more surprisingly, the recorded scores are very close to chance
